interviewQuestions.question: How would you rotate an n x n matrix 90° clockwise in place?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd decompose it into two operations I already trust: transpose, then reverse each row.

**Transpose** swaps `mat[i][j]` with `mat[j][i]` for every pair above the diagonal (`i` from 0 to n-1, `j` from `i+1` to n-1) — each pair is disjoint from every other, so this can be done with simple swaps in place, no second matrix. **Reversing each row** then flips the left-right order within that row.

Why that composition equals a 90° clockwise rotation: transposing moves what should become the new first row into place, but in reversed left-right order; reversing each row corrects exactly that. I'd trace it on a small 3x3 example out loud to confirm before coding.

```python
def rotate_90(mat):
    n = len(mat)
    for i in range(n):
        for j in range(i + 1, n):
            mat[i][j], mat[j][i] = mat[j][i], mat[i][j]
    for row in mat:
        row.reverse()
```

Both passes touch each element a constant number of times, so it's O(n²) time — the best possible, since every element must be examined — and O(1) extra space, since everything happens on the existing matrix.

I'd flag immediately that this only works for **square** matrices — a non-square rotation changes the shape entirely and needs new storage, which I'd rather state up front than have it surface as a bug later.

**Testing:** whether you can produce the transpose-then-reverse decomposition rather than trying to derive index-mapping formulas from scratch under time pressure.

interviewQuestions.question: Two nested loops traverse the same n x n matrix — one row-by-row, one column-by-column. Both are O(n²). Why might one run noticeably slower in practice?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
This comes down to memory layout, not the algorithm. Most languages store a matrix **row-major** — row 0's elements contiguous, then row 1's, and so on, addressed as `base + (i*cols + j)*element_size`.

Row-by-row traversal walks that layout sequentially: each next element is the very next thing in memory, which the CPU's cache prefetcher loves — one cache-line fetch serves many consecutive accesses. Column-by-column traversal jumps `cols` elements at a time between reads, which on a large matrix means each access can land in a different cache line or even a different page, causing a cache miss on nearly every single read.

Concretely, on a matrix large enough that a row doesn't fit in L1 cache, I'd expect the column-major traversal to run several times slower in wall-clock time — same O(n²) element count, wildly different memory-access pattern. This is the exact same gap Big-O deliberately ignores: it counts operations, not cache behavior.

The practical takeaway I'd state: when writing matrix code, match your loop nesting to the storage layout — inner loop over the contiguous dimension — and if working with column-major data (Fortran-derived libraries, some NumPy configurations), flip the nesting to match.

**Testing:** whether you connect an abstract Big-O-equal comparison to a concrete, measurable hardware effect.

interviewQuestions.question: Walk me through spiral matrix traversal, and where candidates typically go wrong.
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I track four boundaries — `top`, `bottom`, `left`, `right` — instead of writing a fresh set of loops for every ring. Each full lap around the current ring does four directional walks: left-to-right along `top`, top-to-bottom along `right`, right-to-left along `bottom`, bottom-to-top along `left`. After a full lap, I tighten all four boundaries inward (`top+=1, bottom-=1, left+=1, right-=1`) and repeat until `top > bottom` or `left > right`.

The bug that trips people up almost every time is the **innermost ring** — a single row, a single column, or a single cell. After walking `top` left-to-right and `right` top-to-bottom, the ring might already be fully consumed: if it collapsed to one row, `top` now equals `bottom`, and walking `bottom` right-to-left would revisit the same cells the `top` walk just covered. The fix is checking `if top <= bottom` before that third walk, and `if left <= right` before the fourth — not just at the very start of the ring, but before *each* of the last two walks specifically.

I'd test this mentally against a 1×n matrix and an n×1 matrix before trusting the code, since those are exactly the shapes that collapse a ring to its innermost case immediately.

**Testing:** whether you can implement a technique correctly on its edge cases, not just its typical multi-ring case.

interviewQuestions.question: A matrix-multiply implementation in production is much slower than expected even though its complexity analysis (O(n³), naive triple loop) matches the textbook. What would you look at?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd assume the complexity class is right and look at memory access pattern instead, since a naive O(n³) matrix multiply is a textbook case of algorithm and implementation diverging in real performance.

The usual culprit: a naive triple-nested loop over `A[i][k] * B[k][j]` accesses `B` column-by-column in its innermost loop if written the obvious way, which on a large row-major `B` means a cache miss on nearly every multiply — the same row-major-vs-column-major gap as simple traversal, just compounded across three nested loops instead of two.

What production numerical libraries (the BLAS implementations behind NumPy, PyTorch, TensorFlow) actually do is **cache blocking (tiling)**: process the matrices in small sub-blocks sized to fit in L1/L2 cache, doing all the work for one block combination before moving to the next, instead of sweeping full rows or columns straight through. This can be a 10-50x wall-clock improvement over the naive loop order on large matrices, despite both being the identical O(n³) algorithm — Big-O doesn't see cache hierarchy at all, and this is exactly where that blind spot costs the most.

I'd check this concretely by looking at whether the inner loop strides across `B`'s rows (cache-friendly) or its columns (cache-hostile), and whether the matrix sizes involved exceed typical L1/L2 cache (tens of KB to a few MB) — if they do, reordering loops or reaching for a BLAS-backed library instead of hand-rolled loops is usually the fix, not a different algorithm.

**Testing:** whether you can reason past Big-O to the memory-hierarchy effects that actually dominate real matrix-heavy workloads.
